analysis.one_liner: Phases out large factory farms by 2040, forces meatpackers onto open markets, and restores meat origin labels.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze the creation and expansion of large factory farms (CAFOs) and shut existing ones down by 2040, while giving their owners federal grants to pay off debt and switch to other farming. It would make big meat and poultry companies legally responsible for the waste and pollution their contract farms produce, force large meatpackers to buy at least half their cattle and hogs on open cash markets instead of through closed deals, and restore mandatory country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy.
analysis.who_benefits: Family-scale ranchers and farmers gain a fairer shot: large packers would have to buy half their livestock through open, competitive bidding rather than formula deals with their own affiliates, and poultry companies could no longer pay growers through opaque "tournament" comparisons or retaliate against growers who speak up [S3]. Owners of existing feeding operations gain access to grants that pay down construction debt and fund a switch to pasture-based or specialty agriculture [S3]. People living near large CAFOs gain the right to sue the corporation, not just the local operator, for health harms, lost property value, and pollution [S2, S3]. Shoppers gain mandatory labels showing where beef, pork, and dairy come from, with "Product of USA" reserved for animals born, raised, and slaughtered here [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars new large CAFOs from starting or expanding and requires existing ones to cease operating as large CAFOs after January 1, 2040, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation per day.
Creates a voluntary program funded at $10 billion per year to pay off feeding-operation debt and help owners transition their land to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production.

Makes integrators — the meat and poultry companies that control contract farms — liable for dead animal and manure disposal, air and water pollution, harm to contract growers and neighbors, and loss of property value, with those duties nondelegable and attorney fees available to prevailing plaintiffs.

Requires covered packers to buy at least 50% of their daily slaughter volume through spot market sales from nonaffiliated producers, limits forward contracts to those with firm base prices and open bidding, and bans packer ownership of livestock except in narrow cases.
Restricts the poultry grower 'tournament' pay system and bars retaliation, coercion, and one-sided contract terms against growers, and expands USDA enforcement authority over live poultry dealers.

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and restricts 'Product of USA' labels to animals exclusively born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators bear the biggest costs: the spot market mandate, forward contract limits, packer ownership ban, and integrator liability would restructure how they buy and control livestock. Large CAFO operators lose the ability to expand and must exit by 2040 unless they shrink. Taxpayers fund the transition program — $10 billion transferred from the Treasury each year, without a sunset date in the text, no congressional appropriation needed [S3]. Consumers could see some meat prices rise as concentrated procurement practices are unwound.

drawbacks.text: The transition program transfers $10 billion from the Treasury every October 1 with no expiration date or annual appropriation, an open-ended federal outlay whose total cost depends entirely on how many operators take the deal.

A freeze on new and expanding large CAFOs, combined with a mandate that half of slaughter volume be bought on the spot market, would reduce supply and procurement flexibility and could raise retail meat prices, at least during the transition — a cost that falls on ordinary shoppers.

The 2040 phase-out draws hard lines at fixed herd sizes (for example 1,000 cattle or 2,500 hogs), so operations just under those thresholds could keep growing right up to the line, and the phase-out could push some production to other countries with weaker environmental rules rather than reduce it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For family farmers, contract growers, and people living beside large CAFOs, the upside is substantial: real legal leverage over the corporations that control their operations, open-market price discovery, and paid exit from debt-burdened factory farms. The costs are real too — an open-ended multibillion-dollar annual transfer to buy out operators, possible short-term meat price increases, and practical enforcement questions around the 2040 deadline. The core design problem is that the bill attacked the most concentrated part of the American food system all at once, which is precisely why it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture and Transportation committees and their subcommittees and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Ro Khanna introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by 18 original cosponsors including Pramila Jayapal, Mark Pocan, and Cori Bush.

The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; days later it went to the subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment and on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.
That was the last action ever taken. Across the two-year Congress the bill received no hearing, no committee markup, no committee report, and no vote in either chamber.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The four large meatpacking companies and the poultry integrators that dominate livestock buying came out ahead: the current closed procurement system, packer feeding, and grower tournament pay all remain intact, and large CAFOs face no new limits.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 18 original cosponsors.

for.name: 39 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Senate companion version of the Farm System Reform Act.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Meatpacking, poultry, and large livestock producer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the CAFO moratorium, the packer ownership ban, and country-of-origin labeling in the public debate over the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached the floor, so no vote ever recorded the parties' positions.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (beef, pork, and poultry processors)
industries.note: The bill would force them to buy at least half their livestock through open spot-market bidding, ban packer ownership and feeding of livestock, and expose them to grower lawsuits. Their current model of buying through formula contracts and their own captive supply is exactly what the bill targets.

Companies that supply chicks, feed, and instructions to contract growers would become liable for farm waste, pollution, and harm to growers and neighbors, and would face limits on the tournament pay system that allocates grower compensation. The bill's nondelegable liability provisions take away the legal firewall between the corporation and the farm.

New large CAFOs could not start or expand, and existing ones must stop operating as large CAFOs by 2040. Operators could instead take federal grants to pay off debt and convert the property, but only by giving up a working-lands easement that permanently bars CAFO use.

industries.industry: Family-scale livestock producers and contract growers
industries.note: Open-market purchase mandates would restore price competition for their livestock, and new rules would bar retaliation, opaque pay schemes, and one-sided contract terms. This is the constituency the bill was written for.
